candidates.summary: isCrossingCurParam dropped the realm-type test, so any function-scope name `cur` in a crossing function whose first realm param is not named `cur` is now unwritable and undeclarable; code that compiled and ran at the merge base is rejected
candidates.failure_scenario: func F(_ realm, xs []int) int { cur := 0; for _, x := range xs { cur = cur + x }; return cur } compiles and prints 6 at b7845fb2d. At 6d88deba7 preprocess panics at the `cur := 0` line with "cannot reassign the crossing `cur` parameter: it names the realm this frame is executing as, and that binding is fixed for the life of the frame". The base rule gated on evalStaticTypeOf(ne) == gRealmType and skipped n.Op == DEFINE; the new helper asks only the name plus the declaring node's IsCrossing(), and the DEFINE carve-out was removed, so an int cursor named `cur` is caught. `func X(_ realm, ...)` is a common crossing shape in examples/. A deployed realm carrying that shape stops preprocessing after the upgrade, so it becomes uncallable with no migration named. Adding `&& ft.Params[0].Name == "cur"` in both arms closes it.

candidates.summary: a named result `cur realm` of a crossing function is refused as if it were the crossing parameter, the case the PR's own fix 2 set out to clear
candidates.failure_scenario: func F(_ realm) (cur realm) { cur = nil; return cur } is refused at preprocess with "cannot reassign the crossing `cur` parameter". The named result is not any frame's identity: installInheritedCur never reads it, and the PR body lists named results as the shape the new declaration test frees. It frees `func F(x int) (cur realm)` (zrealm_cur_other_legal.gno) and misses the crossing-function variant, because IsCrossing() asks only whether Params[0] is realm-typed, never whether it is named `cur`, which the FuncTypeExpr rule leaves free. Same root cause and same one-line fix as the finding above.

Adding `func F(_ realm, xs []int) int { cur := 0; ... }` to that fixture turns it red at this sha and holds the boundary for whichever shape of the rule lands.

candidates.failure_scenario: func Target(cur realm) {} with func F(_ realm) (cur realm) { Target(cur); return } passes the provenance switch, whose FuncDecl arm asks only dft.IsCrossing(). Fail-closed, so nothing is laundered; the cost is a compile-time error surfacing as a misleading runtime abort.
